director.chapterArc: Toren begins by detecting a single impossible error in Rook’s competence, then builds a private case from sleeplessness, misplaced anger, costly care, and physical collapse. The chapter’s center is the involuntary utterance of Vera’s name: intimate evidence that converts suspicion into certainty. Around the fire, observation becomes diagnosis, diagnosis becomes a choice to intervene, and the group turns Rook’s own tactical teaching into a compassionate trap. The final reversal makes Milo—not Toren or Dessa—the terrified point of contact.
director.restraintNote: Keep Original Calder measured, observant, and tactically exact. Rook’s deterioration should register through discrepancies in behavior, not through a generalized tragic tone. Treat the Ember as costly physical work rather than spectacle; let Vera land quietly, without announcing its significance. In the council, preserve calm deliberation even as the implications darken. Any temporary color must resolve fully back into Calder’s warm, grounded base.

cues.delivery: Make Rook’s unraised voice more dangerous than a shout: a precise boundary from a man alarmed by how thoroughly he has been seen, with no theatrical anger.
cues.from: "You were reading me. You've been doing it for a week, all four of you have, and I've let it run because it's a good skill, and I taught you most of it, and I am telling you now to take it off me and put it back on the country where it belongs." He had not raised his voice at all. It was worse than if he had. "You've got no idea what you're looking at. You'll build a whole man out of four days of watching a face, and you'll be wrong in every particular, and then you'll act on it, and you'll do it at exactly the wrong moment because you'll have had a fortnight of being right about husks."

cues.delivery: Let the apology be awkwardly exact and unexpectedly gentle; he is returning responsibility to Milo without asking to be forgiven.
cues.from: Then he walked round the cart and crouched down in front of Milo Faust and said, "That was mine and not yours. There's nothing wrong with the question. Ask it again in a month and I'll answer it."
cues.through: Then he walked round the cart and crouched down in front of Milo Faust and said, "That was mine and not yours. There's nothing wrong with the question. Ask it again in a month and I'll answer it."
cues.reason: Rook reverses the harm and exposes unusual vulnerability.

cues.delivery: Give the medical limits with protective candor: Rook refuses false comfort because accuracy is the only care he can offer, while admitting the cost he has spent.
cues.from: "She's the same as she was yesterday," said Rook. "That's the honest answer, and I want you to hear the whole of it. She's the same as she was yesterday, and yesterday she was worse than she was at Hobb's Wall, and the reason she's the same as yesterday is that I've just spent something on it. That's what that was. It isn't medicine. I'm not a healer, and I've never claimed to be one; I can hold a gate shut for a night, and I can't fix a single thing that's actually wrong with her."

cues.reason: The group learns both Senna’s prognosis and the personal cost of Rook’s intervention.

cues.delivery: Stay hushed and observational; let the wrong boot angle and open hands accumulate into the realization that the seemingly tireless man has simply failed.
cues.from: It was the most shocking thing he had seen in a month, and it took him a moment to work out why. It was not that Rook slept. He must sleep; everybody slept. They had all seen him lie down at some point in the small hours and had all assumed he did something in those hours that resembled sleeping. It was the posture. He had gone over sitting up with his chin down on his chest and one boot out at an angle that no one would ever choose. His hands had come open in his lap, and Rook's hands were never open.

cues.reason: Rook’s vulnerable sleeping posture is a profound visual shock to Toren.

cues.delivery: Read the sleep-talk flat and unshaped, detached from any waking listener; repetition comes from entrapment, not dramatic escalation.
cues.from: "It's the gate," he said, quite clearly, to nobody, at the bottom of a road in the afternoon sun. "It's the gate, it's the gate—"
cues.through: "It's the gate," he said, quite clearly, to nobody, at the bottom of a road in the afternoon sun. "It's the gate, it's the gate—"
cues.reason: Rook relives the gate while defenseless in sleep.

cues.delivery: Place the name quietly beside an absent person, reasonable and close; allow no sob, catch, or retrospective explanation.
cues.reason: Vera’s name is the chapter’s intimate emotional rupture.

cues.delivery: Dessa is presenting evidence, not indulging panic. Build pressure through the accumulating facts, then make the failing lid a calm diagnosis of imminent loss of control.
cues.from: "He's coming apart," she said. "Slowly, and quietly, and in a way you'd only see if you'd been four feet from him every day for a month, which we all have been. He got the lane wrong. He bit Milo's head off for nothing and then said sorry, and he doesn't say sorry, he says that was mine and not yours about nine days after the fact, if ever. He's been facing east for three nights. He hasn't slept properly in a week, and today he went over sitting up in the middle of the day like a man who's fallen off a wall.
cues.through: "And I don't think it started at the camp in the field. I think it started at the Drum ten days ago when Ott said the name, and I think everything since then has been him holding a lid down with both hands, and I think the lid's going."
cues.reason: The group’s scattered observations resolve into a single alarming conclusion.

cues.delivery: Wyck’s family example is plain testimony offered for use; keep the old hurt embedded in practical knowledge rather than foregrounding it.
cues.from: "He's not further off it," said Wyck. "He's closer, and that's what's wrong with him. A man who's got a thing locked up and means to keep it locked up doesn't lose sleep over it; he's had it locked up for years, and it's a room he doesn't go in. This is what it looks like when a man's started going in the room." He flexed the fingers of his left hand. "My mother's the same about my father. Eleven years, and she's fine, and then somebody asks her one civil question at a wake, and she's finished for a month, and it isn't because she's forgotten him, it's because she'd just about got to the point of being able to say his name in the kitchen."

cues.delivery: Forecast Rook’s departure with quiet certainty. The frightening part is that every step would be competent, generous, and irreversible in his own mind.
cues.from: "He offered it out loud, Milo. He offered it three days ago as a solution to exactly this problem, and none of you seem to have noticed that he meant it as a kindness." Wyck put another stick on. "He'll walk us to the gate, and he'll go. And it'll be the worst thing that ever happens to the five of us, and he'll think he's done us a favour, and the maddening thing is he'll have taught us everything he knows on the way, in full, without missing a day, because that's the sort of man he is."

cues.reason: Wyck reveals the likely consequence of leaving Rook alone.

cues.delivery: Make Milo small but morally clear: he agrees to intervene while pleading that their method must not become another injury.
cues.from: "Push," said Milo, in a very small voice, "but not — not at him. Not the way he did the coat. I don't want to do a thing to him."
cues.through: "Push," said Milo, in a very small voice, "but not — not at him. Not the way he did the coat. I don't want to do a thing to him."
cues.reason: Milo defines the compassionate limit of the group’s plan.

cues.delivery: Keep the horror compact and almost breathless. Milo sees the assignment before it is spoken; the final line is tiny, sincere, and faintly human in its awful inevitability.
cues.from: Milo Faust sat on the other side of the fire with his arms round his knees and looked back at them with an expression of absolute horror.
cues.reason: The planned intervention resolves into Milo’s personal burden.
